title: Contact Group 51/49: Sarajevo's Response
sources: Richard Holbrooke, To End a War (Random House, 1998), Ch. 5
Warren Christopher, In the Stream of History (Stanford University Press, 1998), Ch. 7
content:
In July 1994 the Contact Group — the United States, United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Russia — presented its 51/49 territorial framework to all three Bosnian parties on a take-it-or-leave-it basis. The map secured 51 percent of Bosnian territory for the Bosniak-Croat Federation, recognized the RS at 49 percent, kept Sarajevo as a unified capital, and placed the eastern enclaves under the safe-area regime.

For the Sarajevo Presidency the framework was the first great-power map that conceded the principle of Federation parity. Holbrooke's and Christopher's accounts record the US-led shuttle diplomacy that secured the Federation's acceptance: the 51/49 split was less than the unitary state Sarajevo claimed, but it isolated Pale as the rejectionist party and aligned Sarajevo with the Contact Group's coercive leverage — sanctions on the RS, and the looming threat of NATO airpower and a lifted embargo.

Historically the Presidency accepted, calculating that endorsing the plan transferred the burden of rejection onto Pale, whose refusal at the Bijeljina assembly of 3 August 1994 produced exactly the isolation the Contact Group intended — including Milošević's embargo on the RS. The alternative postures were to reject the map and hold the unitary claim, or to accept it with public reservations that preserved a maximalist negotiating position.

The posture recorded here governs whether Sarajevo entered the 1995 endgame aligned with great-power leverage or holding out against it.
